insider_note: The equation is linear in y with P = 1/(xlogx); recognising ∫1/(xlogx)dx as the standard ∫f'(x)/f(x)dx form with f(x) = logx is what lets the integrating factor collapse all the way down to the plain logx instead of staying as e^(log(logx)).

steps.label: Rewrite in standard form and identify P
steps.margin_note: One mark. Divide throughout by xlogx to reach the standard linear form.
steps.memory_tip: logx/logx cancels to 1 whenever the same logx appears top and bottom — always simplify before moving on.
lines: This is in the form dy/dx + yP(x) = Q(x).
steps.why: Dividing every term by xlogx makes the coefficient of dy/dx equal to 1, which is what the standard linear form requires, and it also cancels one logx from the right side, leaving the clean Q = 2/x.
common_mistakes: Dividing only the y term by xlogx and forgetting to divide the right side 2logx as well.
Leaving Q as 2logx/(xlogx) without cancelling the common logx factor.

steps.label: Find the integrating factor
steps.margin_note: One mark. I.F. = e^(∫P dx); recognise ∫1/(xlogx)dx as the f'/f form with f(x) = logx.
steps.memory_tip: ∫f'(x)/f(x) dx = log f(x) is the fastest route whenever the numerator is exactly the derivative of the denominator's inner function.
steps.why: The integrand 1/(xlogx) is exactly f'(x)/f(x) with f(x) = logx, so it integrates directly to log(logx) by the standard log-derivative rule; e raised to a log then cancels back to the plain expression.
common_mistakes: Trying to integrate 1/(xlogx) as a plain 1/x integral and missing the extra logx factor.
Leaving the I.F. as log(logx) instead of simplifying e^(log(logx)) back to logx.

steps.label: Set up the integral and substitute
steps.margin_note: One mark. y·(I.F.) = ∫(I.F.)Q dx; the substitution t = logx removes the awkward logx/x term.
steps.memory_tip: logx/x always substitutes cleanly with t = logx, since d(logx) = dx/x is exactly the leftover factor.
lines: Hence the solution is y·(I.F.) = ∫(I.F.)Q dx
steps.why: Multiplying Q by the integrating factor logx gives an integral in logx/x, and the substitution t = logx turns it into a plain polynomial integral, since dt is exactly the leftover 1/x dx factor already present.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the factor of 2 carried from Q = 2/x.
Missing that dt = dx/x is already present in the integral, and attempting a different substitution.

steps.label: Integrate and finish
steps.margin_note: The last mark. 2∫tdt = t² + c, then substitute t = logx back in.
steps.memory_tip: 2∫t dt = t² directly — the 2 and the 1/2 from the power rule cancel exactly.
lines: So y·logx = t² + c, and putting t = logx back in:
steps.why: The standard power-rule integral of t gives t², and substituting t = logx back in returns the final relation entirely in terms of x.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to substitute logx back in and leaving the answer in terms of t.
Missing the factor of 2 cancelling against the 1/2 from integrating t, and writing an extra 2 in the final answer.
